frameworks.name: The Subconscious Voice Framework
frameworks.definition: Decision paralysis stems from internalized external voices (not your own) that subconsciously control your choices; identifying and dismissing these voices unlocks decision-making velocity.

frameworks.name: The Cost-of-Delay Analysis
frameworks.definition: If you believe you will take an action sooner or later, the rational decision is to take it now to begin capturing benefits immediately rather than postponing.

claims.text: Repeated decision-avoidance creates your current life outcomes. If you have run the cycle of reaching the precipice and choosing not to act multiple times, your present life is the result of those non-decisions.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.mechanism: Each non-decision reinforces the pattern and compounds over time to shape overall life trajectory

claims.text: Delaying a beneficial action you believe you will eventually take is irrational. If the outcome is identical whether you act now or later, acting sooner gives you the benefits for longer.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: You genuinely believe you will take the action eventually
The action has positive expected value

claims.text: Most decision paralysis is driven by internalized external voices that are subconscious and invisible unless actively named. People typically have one or two dominant voices controlling their choices.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
bounded_by: May not apply to individuals with different psychological structures or trauma responses

claims.text: Identifying whose voice is driving a decision (rather than your own judgment) reveals the absurdity of giving control of your life to someone else's opinion. Once named, the external voice loses power.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.mechanism: Conscious awareness of the voice's origin breaks the subconscious pattern and enables choice

claims.text: Alex Hormozi almost did not sell Gym Launch for $46 million because he was concerned that a specific colleague would not find it sufficiently impressive, despite $46 million being a significant outcome.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Peer relationships respected but not family/close friends

claims.text: External voices constraining decisions are typically subconscious; they only become visible when you actively listen for them and name their source.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi

claims.text: People live lives constrained by external judgment (from unnamed people: a colleague, a relative, a peer) and fail to recognize they are giving control over major life decisions to people whose actual influence should be minimal.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Applies to life decisions spanning marriage, business pricing, business exit, major commitments

examples.text: Alex Hormozi hesitated to sell Gym Launch for $46 million because he worried a respected colleague would find the valuation unimpressive. Upon reflection, he realized the voice saying 'John won't think this is impressive' belonged to his colleague John, not his own judgment. Once he named whose voice it was, he recognized it was absurd to let John's opinion control whether he sold a $46 million business or not, and the hesitation dissolved.

The consequences of subconscious external voices can determine life-altering choices: 'Is John really going to be the reason I don't get married to this girl? Is Joe really going to be the reason I don't raise my prices? Is Sarah really the reason why I'm not going to sell this thing?' These examples show the absurdity of letting unnamed external voices control marriage decisions, pricing decisions, and business exit decisions.

practices.text: When facing paralysis on a major decision, ask yourself: 'Whose voice is this? Is this my judgment or someone else's?' Name the specific person whose opinion you are internalizing.
For any important decision you know you will eventually take, execute it as soon as possible rather than delaying, to begin enjoying benefits sooner.

Examine major life decisions (marriage, business pricing, business sale) and ask explicitly: 'Is [specific person] really going to be the reason I don't do this?' to surface whether an external voice is driving the constraint.
